passages.heading: Solving our Affordability and Insurance Crisis
passages.text: The property insurance crisis is the primary reason so many people in Florida are struggling to afford a place to live. From renters to retirees to homeowners, the burden of property insurance continues to make housing costs in Florida unaffordable for many. A state catastrophic fund that removes natural disaster risk from the private insurance market would dramatically reduce property and car insurance rates, restoring affordability and price stability for millions of Floridians. Allowing condominium associations and owners access to a no-interest state-backed loan program would likewise address the crushing financial burden of generational condominium repairs.

passages.heading: Saving Our Schools
passages.text: Public schools have been inadequately funded in the state of Florida for decades. We need to dramatically increase investment in Florida's public schools to provide higher quality public schools in more neighborhoods, with more teachers who earn a more competitive salary. Schools in Florida's private school voucher program need to meet the same high standards as our public schools. Private schools that accept vouchers should be required to provide the same specialized services public schools provide and not charge additional tuition. The voucher program should be means-tested to ensure funding is provided for families with demonstrated economic need.

passages.heading: Campaign Finance and Ethics Reform
passages.text: Florida has some of the weakest ethics and campaign finance rules of any state in the country. Incumbent politicians solicit unlimited money from corporations in clear relationship to official acts. Florida should lead the nation in campaign finance reform and a sweeping ethics package committed to transparency and to protecting Florida taxpayers from legalized graft in Tallahassee.

passages.heading: Strengthening Florida's Economy
passages.text: Florida has one of the largest economies in the world, but it has been hindered by short-term political thinking. Florida should become a leading technology economy and invest in a renewed agriculture economy with a vision for the next century. We should continue to grow our tourist economy and should retain Florida's top talent while attracting the world's brightest minds and creators.

passages.heading: Restoring Reproductive Freedom
passages.text: Reproductive healthcare decisions should be made between women and their doctors, not politicians. Roe v. Wade and Casey v. Planned Parenthood provided a responsible, balanced framework for protecting these decisions. Absent federal legislation restoring these protections, Florida should codify the Roe/Casey framework.

passages.heading: Investing in Climate Resiliency, Clean Water, and the Ocean Economy
passages.text: Florida is home to remarkable ecosystems, waterways, and coastlines. The state's management of these resources has been insufficient. Florida should accept the science of climate change, protect our beaches and state parks, and invest in resiliency throughout the state. Florida should adopt a sustainability agenda that conserves our natural resources and grows an economy reliant on tourism, fisheries, hospitality, and outdoor living.

passages.heading: Restoring Services for Our Veterans
passages.text: Florida is home to one of the largest veteran populations in the United States. We are fortunate to have men and women from all generations who have honorably served across all service branches. In the face of federal cuts and drawback of services, Florida should lead the nation in filling the gap of critical services for those who have served our nation in uniform.

passages.heading: Giving Florida's Families Access to Florida's Universities
passages.text: Too many Florida families are locked out of our state's flagship universities. Florida is fortunate to be home to some of our nation's leading colleges and universities, but it only benefits Florida families if our students can gain admission. Qualified Florida students should have preferred application status for Florida's universities.

passages.heading: Reducing Gun Violence
passages.text: Florida suffers needlessly from gun violence. Responsible gun owners are not the problem, but lax gun laws are. Its time politicians in Tallahassee do more, protecting responsible gun owners' rights while passing common-sense reforms. Florida should ban the sale of assault weapons, require universal and comprehensive background checks, explore licensing, and preserve and expand the red flag laws enacted following the tragedy at Parkland.

passages.heading: Clean Energy
passages.text: Florida leaders should unleash clean and renewable energies across the Sunshine State, requiring greater integration of clean energy technologies into our public utilities. Environmentally sound energy technologies provide for greater stewardship of our environment, protect our tourist and environmental economy, and can drive down utility costs for all Florida consumers.

passages.heading: Home Rule and Direct Democracy
passages.text: Across Florida, voters continue to use their vote to choose the direction of their state and their community. But Tallahassee politicians preempt the will of the voters based on selfish ideological whims. Direct democracy in Florida should be easier, not harder. Florida should respect home rule, and support the implementation of successful voter initiatives in communities across the state. Florida should make constitutional amendments easier for voters to place on the ballot, and if an amendment gets more than 50% of the vote, the Governor should fight to enact it on behalf of the people.

passages.heading: Fighting Crime, not Communities
passages.text: Whether you're a native born Floridian, an immigrant to our state, or a Tallahassee politician, if you break the law in Florida, you'll be held accountable. But Florida can also be a state that corrects disparities in criminal justice for communities of color and immigrant communities, promoting local control of community policing. It's time Florida fights crime, not communities.

passages.heading: Florida Should Be a Place You Can Afford to Call Home
passages.text: From the rent check to the insurance bill, the cost of living here has outrun the paychecks of the people who make Florida run.

passages.heading: Florida Should Be a Place You Can Afford to Call Home
passages.text: Our plan takes on Florida's affordability crisis in several ways. Let's start with housing and insurance.It dramatically lowers insurance premiums by creating a statewide catastrophic fund. It reduces monthly electric bills by capping utility company profits. It scales up workforce and affordable housing construction with down-payment assistance for first-time buyers. Our plan protects renters through expanded affordable housing programs and, to help condo owners cover special assessments, it offers no-interest state-backed loans. It's an actual plan, not an empty promise, to leave Florida families with more money at the end of each month.

passages.heading: The Dream Is Slipping Out of Reach
passages.text: For generations, Florida meant a fresh start, a house with a yard, and the room to build a life. Now young families are watching that promise fade as the typical first-time buyer waits until age 40, and even lifelong Floridians open their insurance bills with dread. This is not just an economic problem. It is about whether working people can still put down roots in the state they love.

passages.heading: Take on the Insurance Crisis
passages.text: No family should have to choose between insuring their home and keeping the lights on. Florida pays the highest homeowners' premiums in the country, and too many carriers have walked away, leaving people stranded. We will fight for a system that treats hurricane risk as the shared statewide challenge it is, so a single storm season doesn't decide whether you keep your house.

passages.heading: Take on the Insurance Crisis

passages.heading: Stop the Runaway Utility Bills
passages.text: Electricity is not a luxury, and over-the-top profits for the biggest utilities should not come out of your monthly budget. Florida regulators have let investor-owned power companies earn some of the fattest returns in the nation while families ration the air conditioning in the summer heat. We will push to cap utility profits in line with the national average and put that money back where it belongs, in your pocket.

passages.heading: Build Homes People Can Actually Afford
passages.text: You cannot fix a shortage by wishing it away, and Florida is short the homes its growing families need. We will invest in the tools that work, from workforce housing to real down-payment help for first-time buyers, so a nurse, a teacher, or a young couple can find a place they can afford. Building more is how we bring prices back within reach.

passages.heading: Protect Renters and Condo Owners Left Behind
passages.text: Half of Florida renters now hand over more than a third of their income just to keep a roof overhead, and older condo owners are being hit with special assessments that can wipe out a lifetime of savings. Safety matters, and no one should live in an unsafe building, but families cannot be left to shoulder impossible bills alone. We will stand with renters and long-time owners so the fine print doesn't force them out of their own homes.

passages.heading: Give Families Room to Breathe
passages.text: When most people can't cover a surprise bill without going into debt, the whole economy is one storm away from crisis. Real affordability means an honest shot at saving, not just surviving the next deductible or rate hike. Every fight on this page comes back to one goal: leaving Florida families with more at the end of the month.

passages.heading: Affordable Once More
passages.text: Florida can be a place where hard work still buys a home, a full fridge, and a night's sleep without worry. Let's build that Florida together.

passages.heading: Q. Why can't I afford to buy a home in Florida anymore?
passages.text: Florida's median home price reached $420,000, mortgage rates sit around 6.36 percent, and insurance premiums are among the nation's highest. Long-term owners pay far less property tax than new buyers for the same house thanks to Save Our Homes caps, and the structural result is that the median first-time buyer age has risen sharply.

passages.heading: Q. How will this plan help me if I rent?
passages.text: More than half of Florida renters now pay over 30 percent of income on housing. The plan scales workforce and affordable housing targeted near job centers, expands existing state housing programs, and caps utility profits to lower the monthly bills renters pay on top of rent.

passages.heading: Q. What if I own an older condo and got hit with a huge special assessment?
passages.text: Older coastal condos have been hit hardest by new inspection requirements, with many owners facing assessments of $50,000 or more per unit. The plan offers no-interest state-backed loans so associations can spread costs over time without forcing fixed-income owners to sell.

passages.heading: Q. What if I am a hospitality worker in Tampa or Orlando?
passages.text: The plan specifically calls for scaling workforce housing based on income and proximity to work, deliberately targeting tourism corridors rather than scattered housing. The utility profit cap would also lower monthly bills, and the proximity to work framing should reduce commute costs.

passages.heading: Q. What are average home insurance premiums in Florida right now?
passages.text: Estimates range from roughly $5,400 to $15,000 per year depending on home value and coverage level. Every credible analysis ranks Florida at or near the top nationally, with coastal markets like Miami-Dade, Tampa, and Jacksonville seeing the largest increases.

passages.heading: Q. Won't capping utility profit hurt investment in Florida's grid?
passages.text: The cap would bring Florida's authorized utility return in line with the national average of roughly 9 to 10 percent. Utilities in other states earning that rate continue to invest in grid modernization and storm hardening, there is no evidence that matching the national norm suppresses investment.

passages.heading: Q. Will a state catastrophic insurance fund just be a taxpayer bailout for risky homes?
passages.text: No, it is a risk-pooling mechanism that lowers costs for everyone by spreading hurricane exposure across all Florida homes. Homeowners still pay for their state hurricane coverage, just at a lower combined cost than today's system where each private insurer prices in huge risk margins.

passages.heading: Q. What about retirees on fixed income in Florida?
passages.text: Retirees face acute pressures from condo special assessments and rising property insurance. The no-interest state-backed condo loan is targeted directly at fixed-income condo owners who can't absorb a six-figure special assessment, and the catastrophic fund insurance savings would also hit hardest for retirees who often pay insurance directly.

passages.heading: Q. Why isn't Medicaid expansion enough on its own?
passages.text: Because expansion provides coverage, but people still need somewhere to actually get care. Jolly proposes a 5-year pilot to dramatically expand community health centers in every Florida county so new enrollees can connect with primary care providers, not just have coverage on paper.

passages.heading: Q. How long would this plan take to actually help me?
passages.text: Medicaid expansion can start within months once the Legislature approves it, with coverage beginning in the first year. Scaling community health centers takes longer, which is why Jolly proposes a 5-year build to create durable access alongside the immediate coverage.

passages.heading: Q. Does this plan raise my taxes as a Florida resident?
passages.text: No. The plan uses Florida tax dollars already being collected, paired with a 9-to-1 federal match. The state share is offset by reduced emergency care costs, lower uncompensated care payments, and increased tax revenue from a stronger healthcare workforce.

passages.heading: Q. How would this plan affect rural Floridians?
passages.text: Rural counties have been hit hardest by healthcare gaps. Jolly's plan scales community health centers in every county, including rural areas where private practices are unviable, and stabilizes rural hospital revenue by reducing uncompensated care through Medicaid expansion.

passages.heading: Q. What if I am a small business owner in Florida?
passages.text: Small businesses struggle to offer coverage because they cannot get the group rates large employers negotiate. Medicaid expansion would let your lowest-paid workers have a coverage option instead of being stuck in the coverage gap, and it stabilizes the market where you and your employees buy insurance.

passages.heading: Q. How does Florida rank for healthcare nationally?
passages.text: Poorly across most measures. Florida has one of the highest uninsured rates in the country at 15.5% for working-age adults, ranks among the worst states for maternal mortality, and has about 266,000 adults shut out of both Medicaid and marketplace subsidies.

passages.heading: Q. What if the federal government cuts the 90% match?
passages.text: The 90% match is set in statute, not annual appropriation, which means it cannot be changed without an act of Congress. Any change would also disrupt 41 states' Medicaid programs, including red states like Indiana and Ohio, which makes a partisan cut politically difficult. Florida could adopt trigger provisions that would automatically roll back expansion if the federal match drops below a certain level.

passages.heading: Q. How would this plan affect Florida hospitals?
passages.text: Florida hospitals would see two direct benefits. First, Medicaid expansion would shift much of the uncompensated care burden to the federal government at the 90% match rate. Second, scaling community health centers reduces preventable ER visits by triaging patients in primary care.

passages.heading: Q. Why are so many teachers leaving Florida?
passages.text: Florida opened the 2024-25 school year with nearly 10,000 vacant positions, including over 5,000 teacher roles. The main reason is pay: Florida's average teacher salary ranks 50th of 51 states nationally (only Mississippi is worse), and teachers also cite high cost of living and Florida's political climate as reasons to leave.

passages.heading: Q. What does Jolly want to do about teacher pay?
passages.text: Jolly wants to dramatically increase teacher pay as part of a 10-year public education renaissance. He proposes redirecting Tourist Development Tax revenue (currently used for convention centers and tourism promotion) toward teacher pay and school infrastructure, which would require legislative change.

passages.heading: Q. How does Jolly plan to fund his education priorities?
passages.text: Jolly proposes expanding the allowed uses of Florida's Tourist Development Tax (over $1 billion per year statewide) to include teacher pay and school infrastructure. His framing: Florida doesn't have a crisis of convention centers, it has a crisis of public education.

passages.heading: Q. What about rural Florida school districts?
passages.text: Rural districts face compounding challenges: shrinking enrollment, higher per-pupil costs, and the most severe teacher shortages (especially in special education, science, and math). Jolly's plan to raise teacher pay statewide would help rural districts compete for talent, and expanded state funding would help them maintain operations as local tax bases decline.

passages.heading: Q. How are Florida public schools currently funded?
passages.text: Florida K-12 public schools are funded primarily through the Florida Education Finance Program (FEFP), which combines state appropriations, local property tax revenue, and federal funds. Florida's per-pupil spending is approximately $12,400, ranking 8th lowest among U.S. states.

passages.heading: Q. Is the federal government taking over education policy?
passages.text: No. Federal funding is under 10% of total K-12 spending, and federal law explicitly gives states control over curriculum, funding, teacher policy, and school choice. State-level governance (governor and legislature) is the dominant driver of school quality, which is why a Florida governor's education plan has more impact on Florida students than any federal change.

passages.text: David Jolly and Gwen Graham have proposed an immediate moratorium on the construction of hyperscale data centers in Florida, and David says they would issue it on their first day in office. His reasons are the strain on Florida's water, power, and natural resources; what these facilities do to the neighborhoods and property values around them; and serious questions about the long term economic payoff that he says have yet to be answered. He also says voters across Florida are telling their leaders they do not want data centers, and that leaders should listen.

passages.heading: Q. What is a hyperscale data center?
passages.text: Hyperscale generally refers to the largest class of data centers, and in Florida the working line is drawn at electrical demand. State law defines a large-scale data center and a large load customer as a single location with an anticipated monthly peak load of 50 megawatts or more, calculated as the highest average load over a 15 minute interval, including colocated tenants at the same site. WPLG Local 10 reported in July 2026 that the many data centers already operating in Miami-Dade County are not hyperscale because none requires 50 megawatts or more. Project Tango was described by its project manager as 600 megawatts across five buildings.

passages.heading: Q. What is a hyperscale data center?
passages.text: The Florida sales tax exemption in section 212.08(5)(r) uses a different and higher threshold, requiring a critical IT load of 100 megawatts or higher plus a cumulative capital investment of at least $150 million.

passages.heading: Q. Are data centers coming to Florida?
passages.text: Some already exist, and more are proposed. WPLG Local 10 reported in July 2026 that dozens of data centers already operate in Miami-Dade County, but none are hyperscale facilities requiring 50 megawatts or more. Project Tango in Palm Beach County would have been the first hyperscale data center in the state if approved, and it was denied without prejudice on July 15, 2026. Other proposals have moved and stalled across the state. WPTV reported that projects in Indiantown, Okeechobee County and Fort Pierce were withdrawn after public opposition, while others remain under consideration on the Treasure Coast.

passages.heading: Q. Are data centers coming to Florida?
passages.text: Lakeland published a proposed 12 month moratorium ordinance in June 2026 and noted the city currently has no large load customers and does not permit data centers under its land use rules. Duke Energy Florida told regulators in September 2025 that it had no large load data center customers.

passages.heading: Q. Did Palm Beach County approve or reject Project Tango?
passages.text: Palm Beach County commissioners rejected it. On July 15, 2026, after a hearing that ran more than 12 hours and drew more than 80 signed up public speakers, the commission voted 5 to 1 to deny the application without prejudice. Commissioner Maria G. Marino cast the only vote against denial. Mayor Sara Baxter recused herself because the county attorney advised that her earlier public statements opposing the project created a conflict in a quasi judicial proceeding. Denial without prejudice means the developer may revise the proposal and submit it again.

passages.heading: Q. Did Palm Beach County approve or reject Project Tango?
passages.text: Commissioners said the applicant did not adequately answer questions about noise, water use, traffic and compatibility with the surrounding area. The property still holds its previously approved entitlements for more than 2 million square feet of warehouse and data center development, which the vote did not change.

passages.heading: Q. Can Florida cities and counties ban or pause data centers?
passages.text: Local governments retain land use authority. Section 163.326, Florida Statutes, created by CS/CS/SB 484 in 2026, states that local governments maintain the powers and responsibilities for comprehensive planning and land development regulation with respect to large load customers, and that a large load customer may not be treated as an electric substation, which would have triggered a streamlined approval process. Local governments have used that authority. Palm Beach County adopted a moratorium on AI data centers in early July 2026, though it did not apply to the pending Project Tango application.

passages.heading: Q. Can Florida cities and counties ban or pause data centers?
passages.text: Lakeland published a proposed ordinance in June 2026 for a temporary 12 month moratorium on applications for data centers and large load customers using more than 50 megawatts a month, with a public hearing set for July 6, 2026, while the city studies land use classifications, development standards and utility impacts.

passages.heading: Q. Will data centers raise my power bill in Florida?
passages.text: Florida law passed in 2026 is designed to prevent that. CS/CS/SB 484 creates section 366.043, Florida Statutes, which requires public utility tariffs to reasonably ensure that each large load customer bears its own full cost of service, including connection, incremental transmission, incremental generation and other infrastructure costs, and that those costs are not shifted to the general body of ratepayers. It also says the risk of nonpayment may not be borne by other ratepayers. Every public utility had to file a compliant tariff with the Florida Public Service Commission by October 1, 2026.

passages.heading: Q. Will data centers raise my power bill in Florida?
passages.text: The commission may approve tools such as minimum demand charges, financial guarantees, minimum load factors and take or pay provisions. Whether those protections work in practice will depend on the tariffs the commission approves and on how utilities apply them, which is why the same bill ordered an independent study of rate impacts due July 1, 2027.

passages.heading: David Jolly's Plan to Cut Florida Homeowners Insurance by 60 to 70 Percent
passages.text: Floridians pay the highest home insurance prices in America because every family is made to pay a private insurer to carry hurricane risk. Jolly's proposal moves that risk into one strong, state-backed fund. Here is how it works, what it costs, and what it saves.

passages.heading: David Jolly's Plan to Cut Florida Homeowners Insurance by 60 to 70 Percent
passages.text: Hurricane and wind risk makes up 60 to 70 percent of a Florida homeowners insurance bill. David Jolly's plan creates one strong, state-backed hurricane fund to carry that risk, so private insurers no longer have to price it into your policy. The fund is built to a financially sound level and backed by reinsurance before it covers anyone, and it is paid for by making insurance companies pay the taxes they currently avoid, along with other revenue that does not put the burden back on homeowners. Based on Insure.com's Florida calculator, that is the difference between $7,136 a year and $2,557 for a $300,000 home: about $4,500 a year, a 64 percent savings.

passages.heading: David Jolly's Plan to Cut Florida Homeowners Insurance by 60 to 70 Percent
passages.text: And the rule that governs all of it: the costs will be lower for Floridians, or we won't do it.

passages.heading: What hurricane risk costs a Florida family today

passages.heading: The problem
passages.text: Floridians are paying the highest home insurance prices in America, and the private market has collapsed. Company after company has pulled out of the state or gone under, and the ones that remain price every policy for the worst storm they can imagine, because in Florida the worst storm is not hypothetical.

passages.heading: The problem
passages.text: The main reason a Florida policy costs so much more than one in Georgia or Ohio is one line on the bill: hurricane and wind. That single risk can be 60 to 70 percent of what a family pays. Every other part of a homeowners policy—fire, theft, liability, a burst pipe—is priced roughly the way it is priced anywhere else.

passages.heading: Jolly's proposal, step by step
passages.text: Instead of forcing every Florida family to pay a private insurer to take on that enormous hurricane risk, Jolly's proposal does four things, in order.

passages.heading: Jolly's proposal, step by step
passages.text: Florida creates one strong, state-backed hurricane fund. One fund, for the whole state, carrying hurricane and wind risk for Florida homes.

passages.heading: Jolly's proposal, step by step
passages.text: The fund is built to a financially sound level and buys backup insurance for catastrophic storms. Coverage does not start until enough money is set aside and reinsurance for the biggest storms is in place. The fund is built first; it does not borrow against a storm that has not happened.

passages.heading: Jolly's proposal, step by step
passages.text: The fund is paid for without putting the burden back on homeowners. Insurance companies would start paying the taxes they currently avoid. Other sources that do not put a burden on homeowners, such as a fee on real estate transactions or existing tourist taxes, are on the table. The Legislature writes the specific funding policy. How the fund is paid for, in detail.

passages.heading: Jolly's proposal, step by step
passages.text: Private insurers no longer have to price hurricane risk into your policy. That is where the 60 to 70 percent savings comes from. The rest of your policy stays private, competitive, and priced the way policies are in other states.

passages.heading: This is a model that already works
passages.text: Florida already has a state catastrophic fund. The Florida Hurricane Catastrophe Fund was created in a special legislative session in November 1993, after Hurricane Andrew, and it has been run and expanded by Republican legislatures for three decades. Right now, that fund only reimburses insurance companies for a share of their hurricane losses. It is a bailout for insurers.

passages.heading: This is a model that already works
passages.text: David Jolly's plan takes a structure Florida has already proven and directs it to the people who actually pay the bills. Does Florida already have a hurricane catastrophe fund?

passages.heading: The guarantee
passages.text: The fund is rolled out responsibly. Coverage becomes available only after a fiscally sound amount of money is set aside and backup reinsurance is in place. The Legislature is involved in creating the specific policies, including the funding.

passages.heading: The guarantee
passages.text: And in the end, the costs will be lower for Floridians, or we won't do it. Simple as that.

passages.heading: Protecting what makes Florida, Florida.
passages.text: David Jolly believes protecting Florida's environment is essential to the state's economy and quality of life. His plan calls for real investments in environmental protection, accelerated clean and renewable energy integration into Florida's utility system, sustained funding for coastal resiliency and water quality improvements, and honest climate planning in state policy. David sees environmental protection as protecting what makes Florida successful: the tourism economy, clean beaches, healthy waters, and the natural beauty that families depend on every day.

passages.text: For families across Florida, the environment isn't an abstract issue. It's part of everyday life. It's the beaches they visit and parks they play in. The water they drink and air they breathe. The places that make this state feel like home.

passages.heading: This is about more than the environment.
passages.text: For David and his family, it's deeply personal. Time spent near the ocean, watching their kids experience the same natural beauty that defines so much of Florida.

passages.text: And yet, too often, protecting it is treated like a secondary concern. Something to debate. Something to delay.

passages.text: But the truth is, Florida's environment isn't separate from its success.

passages.heading: This is about more than the environment.

passages.heading: This is about more than the environment.
passages.text: When that is threatened, it's not just an environmental issue. It's an economic one. It's a quality of life issue. It's a future issue.

passages.heading: This is about more than the environment.
passages.text: Protecting Florida's environment means making real investments. Taking real responsibility. And refusing to treat long-term damage as acceptable.

passages.heading: Q. Is my insurance crisis related to climate?
passages.text: Yes, structurally. Florida's property insurance crisis is driven by hurricane risk, litigation costs, and reinsurance prices, and the hurricane risk component has grown with warming ocean temperatures and rising sea levels. Insurers price policies to absorb rising expected losses, so climate is one of the underlying drivers of the insurance crisis.

passages.heading: Q. Is climate change real in Florida?
passages.text: Yes, and Florida faces some of the most direct climate impacts in the country. Florida's Gulf Coast is projected for 22 to 26 inches of sea level rise by 2050 (about double the U.S. average), and hurricane intensity is rising. The 2024 hurricane season caused over $100 billion in combined damage across the Southeast.

passages.heading: Q. What does David Jolly want to do about clean energy?
passages.text: Jolly's position is to unleash clean and renewable energies across Florida, requiring greater integration of clean energy technologies into public utilities. This means stronger net metering rules to support rooftop solar and accelerated utility-scale renewable buildout. Florida is projected to receive $62.7 billion in IRA-funded clean power investment by 2030.

passages.heading: Q. Aren't climate policies just going to hurt the Florida economy?
passages.text: The economic case runs the other way. Florida's tourism economy ($134 billion in visitor spending, 1.8 million jobs), ocean economy, and saltwater fishing industry ($9.2 billion in annual impact) all depend on a healthy environment. Climate policy in Florida protects the state's largest industries rather than imposing costs against them.

passages.heading: Q. What about Floridians who live in coastal communities?
passages.text: Coastal Floridians face the most direct climate exposure: rising sea levels, more intense hurricanes, and accelerating beach erosion. David Jolly's plan calls for wiser coastal development practices and sustained investment in resiliency, which means living shorelines and hybrid systems, seawalls where necessary and appropriate, raised infrastructure, beach renourishment where cost-effective and sustainable, stormwater drainage upgrades, and building code modernization in coastal counties.

passages.heading: Q. How would David Jolly handle Florida's water quality crises?
passages.text: Jolly's plan ties water quality to broader environmental investment. Blue-green algae crises are addressed by reducing discharges of nutrient pollution to our coastal waters, and springs degradation is addressed through septic to sewer conversions, agricultural runoff rules, and groundwater protection. Protecting Florida's coast requires changing what flows into it.

passages.heading: Q. What about FPL and renewable energy under David Jolly?
passages.text: Jolly's clean energy position would require greater integration of renewables into Florida's utility planning. That likely means stronger net metering rules to support rooftop solar and accelerated utility-scale renewable buildout, pushing FPL and other utilities to expand renewable generation.

passages.heading: Q. Why oppose offshore drilling if it could create Florida jobs?
passages.text: Offshore drilling creates very few Florida jobs because rigs are based out of Louisiana and Texas ports. What Florida loses in a spill (tourism revenue, fishing industry, real estate value, ecological damage) runs to tens of billions of dollars. Florida's tourism economy ($130 billion) and ocean economy ($30 billion) depend on clean beaches and healthy water.

passage.heading: Florida Should Be a Place You Can Afford to Call Home
passage.text: Our plan takes on Florida's affordability crisis in several ways. Let's start with housing and insurance.It dramatically lowers insurance premiums by creating a statewide catastrophic fund. It reduces monthly electric bills by capping utility company profits. It scales up workforce and affordable housing construction with down-payment assistance for first-time buyers. Our plan protects renters through expanded affordable housing programs and, to help condo owners cover special assessments, it offers no-interest state-backed loans. It's an actual plan, not an empty promise, to leave Florida families with more money at the end of each month.

passage.heading: Stop the Runaway Utility Bills
passage.text: Electricity is not a luxury, and over-the-top profits for the biggest utilities should not come out of your monthly budget. Florida regulators have let investor-owned power companies earn some of the fattest returns in the nation while families ration the air conditioning in the summer heat. We will push to cap utility profits in line with the national average and put that money back where it belongs, in your pocket.

passage.heading: Q. How will this plan help me if I rent?
passage.text: More than half of Florida renters now pay over 30 percent of income on housing. The plan scales workforce and affordable housing targeted near job centers, expands existing state housing programs, and caps utility profits to lower the monthly bills renters pay on top of rent.

passage.heading: Protect Renters and Condo Owners Left Behind
passage.text: Half of Florida renters now hand over more than a third of their income just to keep a roof overhead, and older condo owners are being hit with special assessments that can wipe out a lifetime of savings. Safety matters, and no one should live in an unsafe building, but families cannot be left to shoulder impossible bills alone. We will stand with renters and long-time owners so the fine print doesn't force them out of their own homes.

passage.heading: Solving our Affordability and Insurance Crisis
passage.text: The property insurance crisis is the primary reason so many people in Florida are struggling to afford a place to live. From renters to retirees to homeowners, the burden of property insurance continues to make housing costs in Florida unaffordable for many. A state catastrophic fund that removes natural disaster risk from the private insurance market would dramatically reduce property and car insurance rates, restoring affordability and price stability for millions of Floridians. Allowing condominium associations and owners access to a no-interest state-backed loan program would likewise address the crushing financial burden of generational condominium repairs.

passage.heading: Strengthening Florida's Economy
passage.text: Florida has one of the largest economies in the world, but it has been hindered by short-term political thinking. Florida should become a leading technology economy and invest in a renewed agriculture economy with a vision for the next century. We should continue to grow our tourist economy and should retain Florida's top talent while attracting the world's brightest minds and creators.

passage.heading: Saving Our Schools
passage.text: Public schools have been inadequately funded in the state of Florida for decades. We need to dramatically increase investment in Florida's public schools to provide higher quality public schools in more neighborhoods, with more teachers who earn a more competitive salary. Schools in Florida's private school voucher program need to meet the same high standards as our public schools. Private schools that accept vouchers should be required to provide the same specialized services public schools provide and not charge additional tuition. The voucher program should be means-tested to ensure funding is provided for families with demonstrated economic need.

passage.heading: Public education shouldn't be an afterthought.
passage.text: David Jolly believes public education should be Florida's foundation, not an afterthought. His plan focuses on paying teachers what they deserve, investing in school infrastructure and resources, and ensuring every child has access to strong public schools regardless of zip code. passage.heading: Saving Our Schools

passage.text: Medicaid is a critical program for Florida. In the face of cuts from Washington and Tallahassee, Florida should commit to expanding Medicaid and ensuring healthcare for all Floridians.

passage.text: David Jolly's health care plan for Florida expands Medicaid to cover hundreds of thousands of uninsured Floridians and invests in more primary care clinics throughout the state so people can access care when and where they need it, regardless of income. Medicaid expansion can start within months once the Legislature approves it, with coverage beginning in the first year. Jolly proposes a five-year pilot to dramatically expand community health centers in every Florida county so care is available, not just coverage on paper.

passage.text: Rural counties have been hit hardest by healthcare gaps. Jolly's plan scales community health centers in every county, including rural areas where private practices are unviable, and stabilizes rural hospital revenue by reducing uncompensated care through Medicaid expansion.

passage.text: Our plan takes on Florida's affordability crisis in several ways. passage.text: You cannot fix a shortage by wishing it away, and Florida is short the homes its growing families need. We will invest in the tools that work, from workforce housing to real down-payment help for first-time buyers, so a nurse, a teacher, or a young couple can find a place they can afford. Building more is how we bring prices back within reach.

passage.heading: David Jolly's Plan to Cut Florida Homeowners Insurance by 60 to 70 Percent
passage.text: Floridians pay the highest home insurance prices in America because every family is made to pay a private insurer to carry hurricane risk. Jolly's proposal moves that risk into one strong, state-backed fund. Here is how it works, what it costs, and what it saves.

passage.heading: David Jolly's Plan to Cut Florida Homeowners Insurance by 60 to 70 Percent
passage.text: Hurricane and wind risk makes up 60 to 70 percent of a Florida homeowners insurance bill. David Jolly's plan creates one strong, state-backed hurricane fund to carry that risk, so private insurers no longer have to price it into your policy. The fund is built to a financially sound level and backed by reinsurance before it covers anyone, and it is paid for by making insurance companies pay the taxes they currently avoid, along with other revenue that does not put the burden back on homeowners. Based on Insure.com's Florida calculator, that is the difference between $7,136 a year and $2,557 for a $300,000 home: about $4,500 a year, a 64 percent savings.

passage.text: Whether you're a native born Floridian, an immigrant to our state, or a Tallahassee politician, if you break the law in Florida, you'll be held accountable. passage.heading: Home Rule and Direct Democracy
passage.text: Across Florida, voters continue to use their vote to choose the direction of their state and their community. Florida should respect home rule, and support the implementation of successful voter initiatives in communities across the state. Florida should make constitutional amendments easier for voters to place on the ballot, and if an amendment gets more than 50% of the vote, the Governor should fight to enact it on behalf of the people.
